text: The three upper-floor windows were widened from narrow two-pane sashes with heavy trim to wide three-pane windows. (why: Modernisation of the windows for more light; an alteration, not a repair.)
The gable window and the two lower front windows were boarded up with braced shutters (why: the house was left empty or abandoned, perhaps as C filled up)
Unchanged and kept from 2010 to 2020; it is the house that kept growing while its neighbours stood still
Small changes to the board joints on the gable siding, with no change to windows or roof. (why: Possibly a few boards repaired or replaced. This is a very small change.)
The house is now divided into an upper and a ground-floor flat with separate owners.
A lean-to shed was added at the back in 1950, and the front windows were replaced in 1965.
It stayed in good order throughout, with the same shop front and veranda in 2020.
a balcony over the lane is added and the house repainted (why: the owners added it in 2003)
No dated change; paint from 2007 ageing (why: no events recorded)
Between 2000 and 2010 it was vacated and its windows boarded up.
Its ground floor had already been turned into a shop before 1989 (plate-glass shopfront cut across the original window positions)
It was still boarded and empty in 2020, so it has been let go for at least ten years.
A balcony over the lane was added in 2003 by the owners.
Still boarded in 2020, so vacant for at least ten years
A young family bought it in 2007; the boards came down and, with the city's help, it was restored with copies of the old windows still in the gables, and repainted.

The small extra ground-floor opening beside the door on the long side is no longer there; only the door and lintel remain. (why: Infilled or removed in a small alteration; I could not tell what the opening was.)
a balcony over the lane is added, and the house repainted (why: the owners added the balcony and painted with it (2003))

A house on the rock outcrop with a shingle-edged roof and several chimneys. Its gable windows were boarded in 1989 and in 2000, so it had been empty or abandoned for at least 11 years and probably much longer.
Between 1989 and 2000 its ground floor was converted to a shopfront or store front, with a fascia, blank panels and a pair of doors.

In 2007 the boards (X-crossed shutters) over D's three front windows came off and ordinary glazed windows with frames appeared, the attic window and the two ground-floor windows. D went from boarded-up to open. (why: The house was brought back into use after standing empty, with the windows repaired or reopened.)
A shopfront fitted across 2 window bays in the ground floor, with a bakery opening in it (why: owners let the ground floor as a bakery as trade came back to the quay road (1997))
It probably stood empty for some time before 1989, since it was already boarded then.
Already left empty by 1989, with its gable and side windows boarded, and still boarded in 2000.
A bakery shopfront across 2 bays was fitted in 1997 when trade came back to the quay road.

The three narrow, trimmed upper-floor windows on the front were replaced by wider, plain windows with no surround (why: a modernising window replacement by the owner; the ground-floor windows, door hood and flower boxes were left as they were)
Upper-floor windows replaced with copies of the 1879 originals, and the house repainted (why: the upper flat's new owners restored it (1998))

The two ground-floor windows left of the door were replaced by a shopfront: a wide fascia board over a large blank panel, with a small projecting box or sign at its end. (why: A business opened on the ground floor and the house was converted to fit it.)
Before 1989 it was lived in and kept, with no sign of neglect.
The glazed gable window and the two ground-floor windows were boarded up with planks and a diagonal brace. (why: The house was vacated and not kept up.)
Abandoned between 2000 and 2010: the gable and ground-floor windows were boarded with planks.
The boards come off the attic window and the two ground-floor windows, and they are glazed and open again. (why: The house was reoccupied or repaired after standing empty.)
Between 2000 and 2010 it was boarded up and left empty
It was repainted in 1987 by new owners.
Built as a large, prosperous two-storey timber house with a bay, sash windows and a broad pitched roof; in 1989 its ground floor still had the original sash windows.
Nothing visible except slight shifts in siding joints and chimney caps; the windows are still boarded. (why: No repair and no recovery.)
The small lean-to on its side was there already in 1989, so an older addition
The owner died in 1986 and the heirs, living in Oslo, boarded up all windows and doors; the house stood empty and neglected for 21 years, and by 1995 the roof leaked.
Boards taken down, windows replaced with copies of the old ones, house repainted and lived in again (why: a young family bought the empty house and restored it with the city's help (2007))
House left empty and starting to decay (unpainted, unkept) (why: the last owner died in 1993 and the heirs, who live away, left it empty)
Shop (café) closed; the shopfront stays but is empty/dark (why: the café moved to a bigger room on the square as the quay road's trade went up the hill (2009))
The shop stood empty from 1974 to 1988, and the house had no repaint between 1949 and 1996.
Its roof and structure kept sound even while it stood empty.
Between 1989 and 2000 the ground floor became a shop, with a shopfront fascia and projecting sign.
Built as a symmetrical dwelling (central door, a window each side, window boxes), still that way in 1989.
The original 1884 chalet-style house burned down in a chimney fire in 1935 and was rebuilt in 1936 as a functionalist house with a flat roof, so the present house dates from 1936.

Ground-floor front reworked in 1997: the left-hand ground-floor window was filled in with a plain flat panel under a new long fascia board, and the single door became a double door, so the ground floor reads as a shop or garage front. A dark box (sign or light box) sits above it. (why: Looks like a change of use of the ground floor, a shop or store front put in a dwelling front.)
Built 1912 as a two-storey jugend house with a mansard roof for a cannery owner.
After the last owner died in 1993 the heirs living away left it empty and it has not been looked after since
Between 2000 and 2010 it was extended with a glazed veranda and a balcony on the lane side
no deliberate change; it stays boarded and empty, and the roof begins to leak, so it looks worse (why: the heirs cannot agree to sell (1995))
Built 1828 by a fisherman as an empire-style storey-and-a-half house; one of the two oldest on the lane.
A glazed veranda with a balcony above was added on the lane-side corner (why: Extension, perhaps for the shop or the family living above it)
A railing or fence appeared at the left edge of the front, beside the bay and shopfront (why: an added balcony, terrace or safety rail for the shop; I cannot tell exactly what it is)
It stood empty and boarded up in 1989 and 2000, and had probably been vacant for some time before 1989.
Before 1989 it was lived in and kept in order.
Both windows on the gable end are boarded up with crossed planks. (why: The house was vacated and let go.)
A small dark-clad house at the top of the lane, seen only at a distance; it looks lived in and glazed in every year
It was boarded up after a break-in in 2008 and was still empty in 2015
The cafe moved off the quay road in 2009 because trade had gone up the hill; the shop stood empty for years
Before 1989 it was probably a dwelling or a house of some standing that had not yet been converted to trade.

boards come off all windows and doors, new copies of the old windows go in, the house is repainted and lived in again (why: a young family bought the empty house in 2007 and restored it with the city's help)
In 1998 the upper flat's new owners put back copies of the 1879 windows upstairs and repainted; the ground floor kept its 1971 windows
Before 1989 it has no visible later additions, so probably a long-standing dwelling kept in its original form
In 2016 the shopfront was removed and the ground floor became a flat, with windows copied from the 1912 originals as the city's wooden-town rules asked
In 1998 the upper flat's owners restored the upper-floor windows as copies of the 1879 originals and repainted; the ground floor keeps the 1971 windows.
Between 2000 and 2010 a balcony or railing was added at the left bay.
It was kept up the whole time: the roof, trim and upper windows stayed intact and nothing was boarded
It was a shop for at least 1989 to 2010, and the roof, upper windows and walls stayed intact and well kept throughout.
By 2010 it had been reopened and reglazed, so it was reoccupied or repaired, and it stayed so to 2020.
From 2010 to 2020 it was lived in and kept
A balcony over the lane was added and the house painted in 2003
It has been split into upper and ground-floor flats with different owners, which explains the mixed windows
It has an extra ground-floor door or opening on its side wall until 2010, and none by 2020.
Its windows, open before, are now boarded up (why: The house was left empty, possibly when its occupant moved (perhaps down to D, timing only, a guess))
It stayed well kept throughout: roof, upper windows and walls show no neglect, and the owner kept investing in it.

A two-storey extension was added in 2003 on the lane side of B: a glazed ground floor (many narrow panes on the lane side plus a larger window and door bay) with a balcony with a railing on top, running out toward the lane. (why: Owner built on a glazed room or porch with a balcony; looks like an extension for more living or business space.)
Since 2007 it is lived in and kept; original 1828 window design was recovered rather than the 1965 ones.
Balcony added over the lane, and the house repainted (why: owners added the balcony (2003))
The oriel bay and the heavy banded roof look like earlier alterations from before the shop was added.

In 2016 the shopfront was taken out and the ground floor made into a flat with copies of the 1912 windows it had covered, because the city's wooden-town rules asked for it, and the house was repainted; the house is now residential again.
still empty and boarded, with nothing done to it (why: heirs leave it empty (still empty in 2015))
The big plate-glass shopfront and fascia are gone, replaced by ordinary windows (three on the ground floor, one new at the far left) (why: The shop closed and the ground floor went back to housing)
Kept and unchanged from 2010 to 2020
A bakery shopfront was fitted in 1997 when trade returned to the quay road
Built in 1828 by a fisherman as a storey-and-a-half empire-style house on the rock outcrop
The small house closing the view up the lane looks essentially unchanged in 1989 to 2020, with glazed windows and no sign of neglect.
A plate-glass shopfront had already been cut into its ground floor before 1989 (a change of use to a shop) and was still there in 2010.
The ground-floor windows are replaced by a shopfront: a fascia, a blank panel and a double door, with a signboard on the wall above. (why: The house was turned into a shop or business premises.)

The symmetrical house front (central door, a window each side, window boxes) was replaced by a shopfront: a fascia board, blank panels where the windows were, a pair of doors, a door canopy and a dark box (a sign or hatch) above. (why: Change of use from a dwelling to a shop or store; the blank panels read as a shuttered or solid shopfront.)

back wall (facing down the lane) gets new factory 'old style' windows; whole house repainted (why: the ground-floor flat's owner changed the back windows (2011); upkeep repaint (2013). The 2011 change falls just before 2010-2020 if you count from 2010, so it is small)
A plain, well-kept dwelling on the quay road in 1989, with its original ground-floor windows and a bay window on the front.
Still boarded in 2020, with no recovery or repair.
In 1971 all its windows were replaced cheaply.
It has been repainted regularly (1987, 2003, 2017) and stayed in good order.
whole house repainted (first coat since 1949), so it looks fresher and kept (why: the cafe's owners bought the house in 1996 and painted it)
It has been lived in and looked after across the whole period, with no sign of neglect.
Its reopening comes at the same time as E being closed up, so the occupant may have moved from E to D (guess)
Built 1828 by a fisherman as a storey-and-a-half empire-style house on the rock outcrop; the oldest house of the five.
It is an old, plain house with a sound roof and walls in every year; its windows were simple and bare in 1989.
It swapped roles with C: when C was reopened, D was shut.
The front windows gained casings with sills and glazing bars; before, they were plain. (why: A second stage of window renewal, finishing what was begun at the gable window.)
It was still boarded in 2020, so it stayed empty for at least a decade
Between 2000 and 2010 a railing was added at its left side
repainted, the first coat in decades; the cafe stays in the ground-floor shop (why: the cafe's owners bought the house and painted it (1996))
Between 2010 and 2020 the shop closed and the shopfront was taken out for regular windows; the house is residential again
Front windows were replaced in 1965

the shopfront is removed and the ground floor gets copies of the 1912 windows; the house is repainted and becomes a home (why: no one rented the shop after the oil-price fall; owners made it a flat and the city's wooden-town rules asked for copies of the 1912 windows (2016))
It was boarded up (windows and doors) in 2008 after a break-in and was still empty and neglected in 2015, so it is the worst-kept house on the lane through 2020.
The shopfront was removed between 2010 and 2020 and domestic windows were put back: the shop closed.
In 2011 the ground-floor flat's owner fitted factory 'old style' windows in the back wall, which faces down the lane, so that wall is later and not authentic.

A glazed veranda was built on the lane side of the ground floor, with a balustraded balcony on top of it. It covers the old side-wall windows. (why: An extension for more living or shop space, paid for by the owner; it is a clear later addition.)
In 1971 all windows were replaced cheaply, losing the original look
Between 1989 and 2000 its ground floor was converted to a shop (windows replaced by a blank panel, fascia and awning)

In 2016 A's shopfront was taken out: the big dark shop window and the fascia board above it were replaced by two ordinary house windows with frames, one small at the corner and one larger in the middle, alongside the existing window and door. (why: The shop closed and the ground floor was turned back into a dwelling.)
Its windows were renewed in stages: the gable window by 2000, the front windows by 2020. That reads as a steady owner doing a bit at a time.
It was well kept in every year I see, with no damage and the roof and upper floor untouched.
In 1989 a modest two-storey dwelling with window boxes and a front door with a small canopy
It was still boarded in 2020, so it has stood empty for at least ten years.
Built as a three-bay dwelling on the quay road, with an upper-floor oriel bay on the left and a steep roof, with the middle window and the door on the ground floor.
In 1998 the upper flat's new owners put back copies of the 1879 windows on the upper floor and repainted; the ground floor kept its 1971 windows.
no change in look; still boarded and empty, a bit more run-down (why: still empty (2015))

The side facing the lane got an addition. In 2000 it was a plain dark boarded wall with small windows. By 2010 there is a first-floor balcony with a railing and a door onto it, and a glazed ground-floor extension (many narrow panes) under it. The shopfront on the quay-road front is unchanged. (why: An owner's extension or enlargement, perhaps a sun room or cafe space. I cannot tell the purpose.)

The upper window on the side (gable) wall was renewed in 1998: it went from a thin plain frame to a larger frame with a projecting sill and a hood over it. (why: Window replaced or renovated by the owner, ordinary upkeep.)
No repainting or repair is recorded, so the house has had no upkeep for decades and closes the view up the lane in a derelict state.

It was built as a house: the ground-floor windows and door line up under the upper windows. A shopfront with a big plate-glass window and fascia was cut into the ground floor at some point before 1989.
Between 1989 and 2000 its ground floor was turned into a shop, with a sign board and a blank panel replacing two windows
Occupied and kept up in 1989 and 2000, with every window glazed.
In 1986 the owner died, the heirs in Oslo left it empty, and all windows and doors were boarded up.
Built as a modest two-storey house with small-paned sash windows, window boxes and a door hood on the quay road.
The boards came off the gable and side-wall windows, and they are glazed again. (why: The house was re-let or reoccupied and repaired after being left empty.)
It is the best-kept house of the five, repainted in 1987, 2003 and 2017
It kept weathering while boarded, with the cladding and roof lines getting harder by 2000
upper-floor windows replaced with copies of the 1879 originals, and the house repainted (why: the upper flat's new owners restored it (1998))
Between 2000 and 2010 it was reopened, with the windows glazed and the cladding and roof tidied
boards taken off every window and door, new windows copied from the old ones, house repainted; no longer empty (why: a young family bought the empty house and restored it with the city's help (2007))
The small house that closes the view up the lane was lived in and kept in 1989 and 2000, with glazed windows.
It happens in the same decade that D is reoccupied. Residents may have moved from the top of the lane to D, but I only guess that.
All windows and doors boarded up (why: boarded after a break-in (2008))
A cafe opened in the empty shop in 1988 and the owners later bought the house and painted it in 1996, the first coat since 1949
It was rebuilt in 1936 as a two-storey functionalist house with a flat roof, so the present house is the 1936 one
Since 2007 it has been lived in and not repainted (13 years by 2020)
new factory 'old style' windows in the back wall facing down the lane, then the house is repainted (why: the ground-floor flat's owner replaced the back windows (2011); upkeep repaint (2013))
a shopfront across two window bays appears in the ground floor (Quay Bakery) (why: owners let the ground floor as a bakery in 1997 as trade came back to the quay road)
In 2011 the ground-floor flat's owner put factory 'old style' windows in the back wall that faces down the lane, so it is a mixture of real-looking copies and factory imitations; repainted in 2013.
It is the only house of the five rebuilt in a modern style, with no old fabric from before 1936.
Between 1989 and 2000 its ground floor was converted to a shopfront with a fascia board, a business use that it keeps through 2020.
A café opened in 1988 (low rent after the crash); its owners bought and repainted the house in 1996, and the café closed in 2009 when trade moved up the hill.
A balustraded balcony or railing appeared at the left bay, at the left corner of the front. (why: An addition by the owner, probably a balcony or terrace on the bay.)
It was boarded up in 2008 after a break-in, and it was still empty in 2015, so the boards are probably still up in 2020.
Between 2000 and 2010 its windows were boarded up: it was vacated or abandoned
Before 1989 it was a neat house with narrow trimmed windows, flower boxes and a hooded door, looked after by its owners
the house is left empty and starts to look neglected (why: the last owner died and the heirs, who live away, left it empty (1993))
In 1971 all the windows were replaced cheaply, which spoiled its original look.
goes from lived-in to empty and starts to look let go (why: the last owner died in 1993 and the heirs live away)
Between 2010 and 2020 the shop closed and the shopfront was taken out for ordinary house windows, so the ground floor went back to living use.
Kept in repair from 2010 to 2020, with no further change.
a shopfront across two window bays appears in the ground floor, with a bakery in it (why: the owners let the ground floor as a bakery as trade came back to the quay road (1997))
A young family bought the empty house in 2007, took the boards down, and restored it with the city's help, with window copies taken from the old ones left in the gables, and painted it
The boards came off all three gable windows (the loft window and the two lower ones), and they were reglazed. (why: The house was re-occupied or repaired after standing vacant.)
A balcony over the lane was added in 2003 and the house repainted; it was repainted again in 2017, so it is steadily kept.
A cafe opened in 1988 (low rent after the crash); its owners bought the house and repainted it in 1996.
Its front windows were replaced in 1965, so it has non-original windows to the street.
A small gable-fronted house perched on the rock outcrop above the landing; glazed and apparently occupied in 1989 and 2000.
By 2010 a railing was added at the left corner of the ground floor.
It became a shop or business by 2000, with a new shopfront and signboard on its ground floor.
After the owner died in 1986 the heirs, who live in Oslo, left it empty with all windows and doors boarded up; by 1995 the roof leaked
The big shop window and fascia are gone. Ordinary house windows stand in their place, lined up under the upper windows. (why: The shop closed and the ground floor went back to living use.)
Its ground-floor windows gained casings and sills (why: Renewal or repair of the windows, small improvement)

The upper-floor windows on the front were replaced: the narrow two-pane windows with trim surrounds became wider three-pane windows without the surrounds. A window on the side wall changed in the same way. (why: Renovation or window renewal by the owner.)
upper-floor windows change from the cheap 1971 ones to copies of the 1879 originals, and the house is repainted (why: the upper flat's new owners restored it in 1998)
No visible change: still boarded up, empty, roof letting in water (why: heirs cannot agree to sell (1995))
House repainted, first coat since 1949 (why: the café's owners bought the house and painted it (1996))
A railing appeared at A's left corner, on the ground-floor side. (why: A balcony, porch or terrace railing was added, probably by an owner using the shop or flat more.)
It is the longest-neglected house and the one the view up the lane ends on, so the lane's top looks abandoned
Built 1912 by a cannery owner as a two-storey jugend house with a mansard roof; roof and upper windows never changed.
House repainted (why: upkeep (2017))

The gable window and the two windows below it were boarded up with braced planks in 2000. By 2010 all three are proper glazed windows with panes and sills again. (why: Looks like the house stood empty or neglected in 2000 and was repaired and lived in again by 2010. A guess.)
After the last owner died in 1993 the heirs, who live away, left it empty and neglected.
An extra opening beside its door on the long side existed in 1989, 2000 and 2010 and was gone by 2020, so there was a small alteration late on.
It had no extensions and no change of use in these years; it stayed a family house.

Two ordinary ground-floor windows on the front were replaced by a blank panelled shopfront with a sign board above it and a small wall box beside it (why: the ground floor was converted from living rooms to a shop or workshop; the blank panel may mean it is shut or shuttered)
In 1989 and 2000 the house stood shut up, with its side, gable and lower windows boarded; it was vacant or let go.

The plate-glass shopfront and its fascia on the ground floor were removed and replaced by two ordinary domestic windows next to the surviving window and door. (why: The shop closed and the building went back to residential use.)
A chalet-style boat-builder's house from 1884 burned down in a chimney fire in 1935
Built in 1912 as a jugend-style house with a mansard roof by a cannery owner; the upper floor and roof have never been altered
It was lived in until the last owner died in 1993; the heirs live away and have left it empty.
Between 2000 and 2010 it was reoccupied or repaired: the boards came off and the windows were glazed again.
Since 2007 nothing more is recorded, so it is presumably lived in and kept.
Built 1879 by a cooper as a storey-and-a-half chalet-style house; roof never changed.
The window in the gable end gained a casing with a projecting sill; the front windows stayed plain. (why: Piecemeal window renewal or repair by the owner.)
It has been kept up since 2010; its windows are glazed in 2010 and 2020.
In 1931 the widow let the ground floor as a shop: a shopfront across 2 bays covered the original windows; an ironmonger traded there until 1974.
Between 2010 and 2020 the owner fitted casings and sills to its ground-floor windows, a modest renewal
It traded as a shop through 1989, 2000 and 2010

The two ground-floor sash windows at the left were replaced by a blank shopfront: a wide fascia, a plain panel below it and a projecting sign bracket. (why: Conversion of the ground floor to a shop or other commercial use.)
all windows and doors boarded up (why: boarded after a break-in in 2008)
The cafe left in 2009 for the square because the quay road's trade had gone up the hill, leaving the shop empty.
The bay window on the upper floor looks like part of the original house; I see no sign that it was added or changed.
It was a lived-in small house with open windows in 1989 and 2000.
A small old house with a large shingled roof, set on a high plinth beside the landing; the plain windows of 1989 look like the original ones.

Shopfront removed; the ground floor became a home with copies of the 1912 windows; house repainted (why: no one rented the shop after the oil-price fall, so the owners made a flat; the city's wooden-town rules asked for copies of the 1912 windows (2016))
It has no visible change after 2000; the front, ground floor, roof and canopy are stable.

A stroke is tagged 1993 on E but I could not see anything change on E in any view (at most a very slight darkening of the siding, and that could be my imagination). I am not claiming a change. (why: unsure)
Roof and upper windows never changed, and the house looks maintained throughout.
Between 2000 and 2010 it was repaired and reoccupied: the boards came off and the windows were glazed.
The metal-looking roof is probably a later re-roofing, from before 1989.
It has not changed since 2000 and stays well kept
stays empty and boarded but decays further; the roof now lets in water (why: heirs cannot agree to sell (1995))
In 1989 it was a plain, tidy dwelling with flower boxes and an ordinary front door.
A plain, simple house on a stone base beside the landing, with its roof and walls untouched across the whole period
The two front windows get a lintel and a sill with feet, like the gable window already had. (why: The window renewal that began in the 1990s was carried on to the front.)
A young family bought it in 2007, took the boards down, restored it with the city's help with window copies based on the old windows left in the gables, and repainted it.
In 1931 the cannery owner's widow let the ground floor as a shop and a shopfront was fitted across two bays; Vik Jernvare ironmongers traded there until 1974.
The boarded windows (gable window, side windows and the lower window at the front) were opened and glazed again. (why: The house was reoccupied or repaired after standing shut up.)
Still empty and boarded, decaying further (why: still empty (2015))
Its windows (an upper and a lower one) went from glazed to boarded. (why: The house was vacated and left empty.)
Between 2000 and 2010 it was closed up, with all lane-side windows boarded, so it was vacated or abandoned.
all windows and doors boarded up (why: boarded after a break-in (2008))
The house has been kept in good repair all through; no boarding, damage or sagging is visible in any year.
Built 1826 by a fisherman as an empire-style storey-and-a-half house, the oldest of the five, closing the view at the top of the lane.
The boards came off its windows and they are open and glazed again (why: Someone reoccupied and repaired the house)
Before 1989 it was already empty: its side and gable windows were boarded in 1989 and 2000
Between 2000 and 2010 it was vacated: its windows were boarded.
Its windows were renewed in two steps: the gable window got a casing by 2000 and the front windows got casings by 2020.
The front windows were replaced in 1965 with new ones to the street.
An extra ground-floor door or opening on the side wall of the house at the top of the lane is gone. (why: It was probably walled in or removed.)
A glazed veranda with a balcony above is built onto the side wall facing the lane. (why: The owner expanded the premises, probably as the shop did well; this is new building, not repair.)
A small house at the top of the lane that is glazed and shows no neglect in any year.
Between 1989 and 2000 its upper-floor windows were replaced with wider plain ones, a modernisation
It was repainted in 1998 and 2013 and is well kept.
It probably stood empty for some years before 1989, since it was already shut up then.
The boarding moved from D to E between 2000 and 2010, so one household may have moved from E to D.
The boarded side and gable windows look slightly more weathered, with harder board and roof lines (seen from the steps only) (why: the house stayed empty and boarded, so it kept weathering)
Between 2000 and 2010 the boards were taken down and the windows reglazed: it was repaired or re-occupied.
It stayed boarded and unrepaired through 2020.
The small gable window gets a casing and a sill with feet where it was bare before. (why: A first step in renewing the windows, as in a repair run.)
In 1931 the cannery owner's widow let the ground floor as a shop and a shopfront was fitted; an ironmonger ran it until he retired in 1974

Ground floor of the front was turned into a shopfront. In 1989 it had a plain wall, a door under a small flat canopy and two small windows with flower-box sills. By 2000 there is a deep fascia board across the front, a big plain panel where the left window was, the door sits in a framed surround, and a dark box (sign or light) hangs on the wall to the right of the door. The upper floor looks the same. (why: Probably a change of use: the house was made into a shop or business. That is a guess from the look.)
Built in 1879 by a cooper as a storey-and-a-half chalet-style house
Its upper windows were renewed in the 1990s, wider and plainer than the old narrow two-pane ones with surrounds.
repainted (why: upkeep (2017))
After that it was unchanged and kept in order through 2020.
Boarded up in 1989 and still boarded in 2000: empty and abandoned for at least eleven years, probably longer

the shopfront is removed and the ground floor becomes a home with windows copied from the 1912 ones; repainted (why: no one rented the shop after the oil-price fall, so the owners made a flat, and the city's rules for the wooden town asked for copies of the old windows (2016))
Its upper windows were enlarged between 1989 and 2000 to wide three-pane openings; a modernisation, not a repair.
The shop stood empty from 1974 to 1988 and the house was unpainted from 1949 to 1996, so it probably looked tired in the 1980s.
A simple swap of occupancy with C: C became occupied as D became empty
All three windows on the lane gable (one in the gable, two below) went from glazed to boarded with braced shutters. (why: The house was vacated or abandoned and closed up.)
the cafe leaves and the shop in the ground floor stands empty (shopfront still there) (why: the cafe moved to a bigger room on the square as the quay road's trade went up the hill (2009))
Between 2000 and 2010 the boards were removed and the windows reopened: someone moved in and repaired it
Built in 1826 by a fisherman as a small storey-and-a-half empire-style house at the top of the lane
Built 1826 by a fisherman as a small storey-and-a-half empire-style house at the top of the lane; the oldest house of the five.
In 2011 the ground-floor flat's owner fitted factory 'old style' windows in the back wall facing down the lane, then the house was repainted in 2013
